# Corridor Planning Study: New York City to Chicago Intercity Passenger Rail

> **Illustrative estimates: costs, schedules and funding figures in this draft come from an uncalibrated planning model and approximate program parameters. They are not budgets or engineering estimates.**

## Executive Summary

This study evaluates three conceptual alternatives for connecting New York City, NY to Chicago, IL via intercity passenger rail: the Lake Shore corridor upgrade (Alternative 1), the Pennsylvania corridor upgrade (Alternative 2), and the New direct high-speed alignment (Alternative 3). Capital cost metrics presented are illustrative estimates derived from 5000 simulation runs per alternative and do not constitute construction budgets. Evaluated trade-offs demonstrate distinct performance characteristics across route length, existing infrastructure use, station density, and delivery duration without establishing an overall preferred alternative.

Alternative 1 spans 954 miles with 11 stations, utilizing a 99.7% share on existing rail corridors. Alternative 2 measures 858 miles across 6 stations, featuring a 99.9% share on existing rail corridors, a median (P50) illustrative capital cost of $24.3B, and a median (P50) delivery duration of 15.8 years. Alternative 3 establishes a 743 miles greenfield route with 2 stations, requiring 571 miles of new track length and carrying a median (P50) illustrative capital cost of $35.5B. Population proximity figures reflect 2020 Census counts rather than projected ridership demand, and alignment over existing corridors does not convey access, capacity, or operating approval.

## Corridor Description

The evaluated alternatives offer distinct operational routing approaches between New York City and Chicago. Alternative 1, the Lake Shore corridor upgrade, utilizes an upgrade of the existing water-level route via Albany, Buffalo, Cleveland, and Toledo. It extends 954 miles with 3 miles of new track length, achieving 99.7% share on existing rail corridors. It serves 11 stations—New York City, Poughkeepsie, Albany, Utica, Syracuse, Buffalo, Erie, Cleveland, Toledo, South Bend, and Chicago—encompassing 22.23 million residents within 10 miles of the line and 7.41 million residents within 10 km of stations.

Alternative 2, the Pennsylvania corridor upgrade, upgrades the Northeast Corridor, Keystone Corridor, and former Pennsylvania Railroad main lines via Philadelphia, Harrisburg, Pittsburgh, and Fort Wayne. It totals 858 miles with 1 miles of new track length and 99.9% share on existing rail corridors. Serving 6 stations (New York City, Philadelphia, Harrisburg, Pittsburgh, Fort Wayne, and Chicago), its catchment includes 22.33 million residents within 10 miles of the line and 7.54 million residents within 10 km of stations.

Alternative 3, the New direct high-speed alignment, adopts a greenfield route across Pennsylvania and Ohio to deliver a 743 miles alignment serving 2 stations (New York City and Chicago). It requires 571 miles of new track length with a 23.1% share on existing rail corridors. Its catchment comprises 16.14 million residents within 10 miles of the line and 5.31 million residents within 10 km of stations. Alignment proximity does not indicate passenger ridership, and existing corridor use does not denote operating permissions.

## Cost and Schedule Range

Capital costs and implementation timelines represent illustrative estimates modeled through 5000 simulation runs rather than engineering budgets. For Alternative 1, the illustrative capital cost ranges from a P10 value of $20.3B to a median (P50) of $25.2B and a P90 of $31.4B. The projected time to opening for Alternative 1 is estimated at a P10 of 15.4 years, a median (P50) of 17.8 years, and a P90 of 20.3 years.

Alternative 2 exhibits an illustrative capital cost range from a P10 of $19.7B to a median (P50) of $24.3B and a P90 of $30.2B. Estimated time to opening spans a P10 of 13.8 years, a median (P50) of 15.8 years, and a P90 of 17.9 years. The route requires capital upgrades along existing rights-of-way while crossing 11 river crossings and 10 environmental flag entries.

Alternative 3 requires substantial civil works for greenfield development, yielding an illustrative capital cost estimated at a P10 of $29.6B, a median (P50) of $35.5B, and a P90 of $42.2B. Its time to opening spans a P10 of 15.9 years, a median (P50) of 18.0 years, and a P90 of 20.2 years, with construction involving 5 miles of new track in flagged areas, 7 environmental flag entries, and 5 river crossings.

## Funding Strategy

Project development would rely on multi-tiered federal programs coordinated through an interstate compact or multi-state sponsorship. For Alternative 1 and Alternative 2, multi-state cooperation must bridge five states (IL, IN, NY, OH, PA) and four states (IL, IN, NY, PA), respectively, while Alternative 3 spans two states (IL, NY). Initial planning could enter through the FRA Corridor Identification and Development Program (Corridor ID), providing Step 1 scoping funds of about $500K to enter the federal project development pipeline.

Core capital execution would target the FRA Federal-State Partnership for Intercity Passenger Rail (National), offering up to an 80% federal share, though typical grant maximums of $3.0B require phasing total median (P50) costs. Under Alternative 2, an additional $2.1B may be pursued via the Federal-State Partnership for Intercity Passenger Rail (Northeast Corridor) due to the 91 miles segment between New York and Philadelphia. Discrete segment works, grade separations, and sidings align with FRA Consolidated Rail Infrastructure and Safety Improvements (CRISI) grants, which top out near $250M.

Non-federal match requirements could utilize Railroad Rehabilitation and Improvement Financing (RRIF) loans, which require dedicated repayment streams such as state appropriations or farebox revenue. Local station elements across the routes could also compete for USDOT BUILD grants, which are capped near $25M per award.

## Risks

Project implementation faces technical, institutional, and environmental risks, including the following considerations:

* Governance complexity: Alignments span multiple state boundaries, requiring complex interstate governance compacts to coordinate capital matches and program delivery.
* Unmodeled operational factors: Analyses have not modeled host railroad agreements, track capacity, freight conflicts, train paths, service frequency, timetable, span of service, or on-time performance and reliability.
* Financial exclusions: Estimates do not budget for rolling stock, maintenance facilities, electrification infrastructure, operating and maintenance costs, farebox revenue, or annual operating subsidies.
* Alignment constraints: Existing corridor alignment does not grant access permissions or track capacity from host freight carriers, while Alternative 3 requires extensive greenfield right-of-way acquisition.

## Next Steps

To advance the corridor toward formal evaluation, project sponsors should execute several critical steps:

* Advance governance agreements: Form a multi-state working group or interstate compact to represent corridor states and submit applications for the FRA Corridor ID Program.
* Complete operational analysis: Model travel times, door-to-door transit competitiveness, service frequency, timetable options, train dispatching simulations, and host railroad capacity constraints.
* Execute travel demand forecasts: Conduct formal ridership modeling, station-pair demand forecasts, revenue projections, and full benefit-cost analyses.
* Define system assets: Complete preliminary engineering to establish rolling stock parameters, maintenance facility locations, traction power and electrification requirements, and detailed environmental impact evaluations.
